# PIXELCRAFT ARMORY — MASTER PROJECT CONTEXT
This document is the portable knowledge base for the Pixelcraft Armory project.
Purpose: allow a fresh Antigravity workspace on another laptop to understand the system, its architecture, its competition workflow, its constraints, its two-round competition model, and how future work must be performed.
This document is intentionally operational rather than promotional.
It distinguishes implemented behavior from intended behavior and records the known architecture from Phases 1–14.
Generated as a transfer manual on 2026-09-29.
IMPORTANT: the actual source code remains the ultimate implementation authority. This document is a contextual guide and must never be treated as a replacement for inspecting source files.


# 0. READ THIS FIRST
1. Treat the existing repository as an existing product, not a blank project.
2. Do not rewrite working subsystems merely because a different implementation is possible.
3. Before changing anything, inspect the relevant existing module and reuse it.
4. Preserve the registered 3D asset library, design-token systems, Three.js/React Three Fiber architecture, AI validation boundaries, backend persistence layer, workspace isolation, and competition workflow unless a task explicitly requests a change.
5. The Armory is the tool/workbench.
6. WORKSPACE is where actual competition prototypes and independent UI/UX work live.
7. Competition projects have two rounds. Round 1 and Round 2 must remain independently traceable.
8. Never let a prototype-specific experiment contaminate the core Armory.
9. Never let an AI response directly execute arbitrary code.
10. AI advises; validators constrain; the user approves; the renderer applies.
11. Use tests and production build checks after meaningful modifications.
12. If a claim is not supported by repository code or documented project evidence, label it as an assumption rather than inventing it.


# 1. SYSTEM MISSION
Pixelcraft Armory is a rapid competition website assembly and design-prototyping environment.
The central idea is to compress the path from an unknown competition brief to a visually coherent, explainable, validated, responsive prototype.
The system combines:
- competition brief analysis;
- visual strategy generation;
- a curated 3D asset registry;
- VisualKit/visual recipe intelligence;
- PixelScreenConfig-based screen composition;
- live Three.js/React Three Fiber rendering;
- AI assistant reviews;
- guarded AI configuration mutation;
- structured research;
- backend persistence;
- project/version snapshots;
- semantic visual diffs;
- competition audits;
- demo/presentation mode;
- export/import;
- isolated workspace management.
The architecture is deliberately layered so that intelligence does not bypass validation and rendering does not depend on uncontrolled model output.


# 2. CORE DESIGN PHILOSOPHY
The governing pipeline is:
RAW BRIEF -> ANALYSIS -> RESEARCH -> STRATEGY -> ASSET -> CONFIG -> VALIDATE -> CANVAS -> PERSIST -> SNAPSHOT -> AUDIT -> PRESENT.

The AI safety and control philosophy is:
AI ADVISES -> ARMORY VALIDATES -> USER DECIDES -> PIXELCOMPOSER RENDERS.

The system should never become:
AI GENERATES CODE -> CODE EXECUTES -> CANVAS CHANGES WITHOUT REVIEW.

The reason for this separation is both security and predictability.
A language model can produce useful recommendations, but its output is not trusted configuration merely because it is syntactically valid JSON.
The Armory validates the semantic values against known registries and constraints.
The user remains the final authority over design mutations.


# 3. TECHNOLOGY STACK
Frontend:
- React-based application.
- TypeScript.
- Vite build tooling.
- Three.js.
- React Three Fiber.
- Drei.
- Framer-related animation dependencies.
- Leaflet for GIS/map-oriented functionality.
- Lucide icon package.
- CSS/design-token based styling and project-specific UI components.

Backend:
- Node.js.
- Express-style HTTP server.
- TypeScript.
- REST API under /api/*.
- MySQL persistence when available.
- In-memory persistence fallback when MySQL is unavailable.

AI:
- Google Gemini integration for real AI competition coaching.
- Documented model: gemini-2.0-flash.
- Structured JSON-oriented AI output.
- MockAIProvider deterministic fallback.
- AIOrchestrator for multi-role review.
- AIChangeValidator for guarded mutations.

Persistence:
- MySQL schema with ten documented tables.
- In-memory fallback.
- Frontend LocalStorage fallback through apiClient.

Build:
- npm run lint -> TypeScript no-emit verification.
- npm run build -> TypeScript project build plus Vite production build.
- npx tsx scratch/test_phaseXX.ts -> phase-specific automated suites.


# 4. BACKEND ARCHITECTURE
The backend is a Node/Express-oriented REST layer under server/.
The backend provides server-side services for:
- project CRUD;
- version snapshots;
- version restore;
- visual diff computation;
- Gemini review;
- Gemini Ask commands;
- structured AI research;
- pre-flight competition auditing;
- health/readiness/liveness reporting.

Known API routes from the Phase 10/13 documentation include:
GET /api/status
GET /api/projects
POST /api/projects
GET /api/projects/:id
PUT /api/projects/:id
DELETE /api/projects/:id
POST /api/projects/:id/duplicate
GET /api/projects/:id/versions
POST /api/projects/:id/versions
POST /api/projects/:id/restore/:versionId
GET /api/versions/compare/:v1Id/:v2Id
POST /api/ai/review
POST /api/ai/ask
POST /api/ai/research
POST /api/audit/check
GET /api/health
GET /api/health/readiness
GET /api/health/liveness

The exact current route implementation in source code takes precedence over this list.


# 5. BACKEND PERSISTENCE MODEL
The documented MySQL schema contains ten tables:
1. competition_projects
2. project_versions
3. competition_audits
4. visual_recipes
5. registered_3d_assets
6. asset_licenses
7. theme_presets
8. ai_research_cache
9. ai_change_logs
10. competition_submissions

The database is not supposed to be a single point of failure for the design workflow.
When MySQL is unavailable, the backend can switch to an in-memory database.
The frontend apiClient also has LocalStorage resilience for projects and versions.
This means the intended user experience can continue during development without requiring a live MySQL server.

Do not remove the fallback path merely to simplify deployment.
The fallback is an explicit resilience feature.


# 6. FRONTEND API CLIENT
apiClient is the bridge between UI/engine code and the backend.
Its documented responsibilities include:
- project listing;
- project creation;
- project detail retrieval;
- project updates;
- project deletion;
- duplication;
- version listing;
- version creation;
- restore;
- visual version comparison;
- AI review;
- Ask the Armory;
- AI research;
- competition audit.

The documented ProjectSummary contains identifiers, name, slug, prompt, target audience, industry, active theme, layout count, model count, current version, and timestamps.
ProjectDetail extends this with canvas state, requirement matrix, and visual strategy metadata.
ProjectVersion contains version number, name, description, theme snapshot, canvas state, creator, and timestamp.
VersionDiff contains theme change information, added/removed/modified sections, added/removed models, and a summary.
ResearchResponse is structured into facts, analysis, recommendations, uncertainties, sources, timestamp, and execution time.


# 7. AI ARCHITECTURE
The AI subsystem is provider-based.
The core interface is IAIProvider.
The documented provider operations include:
- reviewDesign(context)
- reviewStrategy(context)
- reviewUX(context)

The system has:
- MockAIProvider: deterministic local behavior.
- GeminiAIProvider: real Google Gemini integration.
- AIOrchestrator: coordinates independent assistants and provider behavior.
- AIChangeValidator: validates proposed configuration mutations.
- assistantRoles: definitions for Design Assistant, Competition Strategist, and UX Reviewer.
- aiTypes: shared AI contracts.
- structured Ask the Armory response handling.

The provider abstraction is intentional.
UI components should not need to know whether the current provider is Gemini or Mock.


# 8. GEMINI INTEGRATION
The documented Gemini provider uses gemini-2.0-flash.
The provider receives a system context containing live configuration state such as:
- title;
- active theme;
- hero layout;
- hero 3D asset ID;
- hero visual size;
- section count;
- active competition brief.

It also receives the valid registered 3D asset IDs from assetRegistry.
The system context lists allowed themes and allowed hero layouts.
The model is explicitly instructed not to output raw executable code.
The expected interaction is structured JSON that describes:
- problem;
- recommendation;
- rationale;
- mutation/diff information;
- confidence and related metadata as supported by the current interface.

Gemini grounding metadata may be captured where available.
The system can attach web-source metadata when the provider response contains grounding chunks.


# 9. GEMINI SECRET HANDLING
There are two historical implementation descriptions in the project records:
- Phase 9 documented a client-side VITE_GEMINI_API_KEY path for direct Gemini provider availability.
- Phase 10 and later explicitly introduced a secure server-side Gemini bridge and documented zero client-side secret isolation, with GEMINI_API_KEY maintained on the server.

For a fresh environment, prefer the later Phase 10+ architecture as the intended production architecture.
Do not move a server secret into a Vite client bundle.
Do not hardcode API keys.
Do not commit secrets to Git.
If source code and older documentation appear to disagree, inspect the current implementation and use the secure server-side bridge as the production model unless the task explicitly concerns historical Phase 9 behavior.


# 10. AI FAILURE BEHAVIOR
Gemini is not treated as mandatory for basic Armory operation.
If the Gemini key is missing, invalid, unavailable, rate-limited, timed out, or unreachable, the system can fall back to MockAIProvider or local heuristic behavior depending on the pathway.
The UI should remain usable rather than crashing.
A provider failure should not erase the current design state.
Multi-assistant review uses independent failure boundaries.
Phase 12 explicitly verified Promise.allSettled-based isolation so one assistant failure does not cascade into the others.


# 11. AI CHANGE VALIDATOR
AIChangeValidator is a security and integrity boundary.
Its job is not to judge whether a design is beautiful.
Its job is to determine whether a proposed AI mutation is structurally and semantically allowed.

Known validation boundaries include:
- allowed property paths;
- allowed theme IDs;
- allowed hero layout IDs;
- registered 3D model IDs;
- semantic design tokens;
- text sanitization;
- section count clamping;
- rejection of script injection;
- rejection of inline executable code.

Phase 12 added explicit HTML/script sanitization and clamps section mutations to a maximum of 12 items.
The validator must remain strict.
If Gemini invents a model ID, the mutation is rejected.
If Gemini invents a theme ID, the mutation is rejected.
If a title contains script injection, the unsafe content is sanitized/rejected according to the validator's current implementation.


# 12. REGISTERED ASSET RULE
The Armory has a curated 3D asset registry.
The documented count is 28 registered production 3D models in the later system.
Older Phase 8 documentation referenced 25 models before later expansion.
The current later-stage count is 28.
Do not manually invent asset IDs.
Use assetRegistry as the source of truth.
Visual strategy and AI providers should select from registered assets.
Asset integrity is part of the competition audit.

# 15. BRIEF ANALYZER
BriefAnalyzer transforms freeform competition language into structured competition analysis.
Its responsibilities include:
- keyword extraction;
- theme inference;
- layout inference;
- GIS/map necessity detection;
- section recommendations;
- semantic understanding of competition requirements.

It is not the final renderer.
Its output feeds VisualStrategyGenerator and CompetitionWorkflowEngine.
Unknown or generic briefs must resolve safely to a fallback strategy rather than crashing.


# 16. VISUAL STRATEGY GENERATOR
VisualStrategyGenerator converts structured competition analysis into visual directives.
It can determine:
- visual theme;
- hero layout;
- 3D hero selection;
- section ordering;
- map/GIS inclusion where justified;
- visual emphasis.

The strategy generator must select only registered 3D assets.
The asset selection rationale is surfaced in the command center and presentation layer.
The purpose is to make asset choice explainable rather than arbitrary.


# 17. VISUAL KIT ENGINE
VisualKitEngine is the bridge from high-level strategy to production-ready screen configuration.
It provides palette/material harmony and visual recipe behavior.
It works with registered assets and design tokens.
It contributes to PixelScreenConfig generation.
When the project needs a new design system behavior, inspect existing VisualKitEngine functionality before creating another parallel visual system.


# 18. COMPETITION WORKFLOW ENGINE
CompetitionWorkflowEngine is the central state controller introduced in Phase 11.
Its documented conceptual chain is:
RAW BRIEF
-> ANALYSIS
-> RESEARCH
-> STRATEGY
-> ASSET
-> CONFIG
-> VALIDATE
-> CANVAS
-> PERSIST
-> SNAPSHOT
-> FINAL AUDIT

It coordinates existing engines rather than duplicating them.
It reuses BriefAnalyzer, VisualStrategyGenerator, VisualKitEngine, DesignValidator, AIOrchestrator, and apiClient.
This engine is the correct place to reason about the complete competition lifecycle.


# 19. DESIGN VALIDATOR
DesignValidator provides factual design/competition checks.
Known areas include:
- requirement coverage;
- contrast;
- spacing;
- viewport scaling;
- structural correctness;
- design issue detection;
- auto-fix mutations.

It should not be confused with AIChangeValidator.
DesignValidator checks the resulting design/configuration.
AIChangeValidator checks whether an AI-proposed mutation is allowed.
Both are necessary.


# 20. EIGHT-DIMENSION COMPETITION AUDIT
The later competition audit uses eight dimensions:
1. Requirements & Brief
2. Visual Structure
3. Responsive Readiness
4. Asset Integrity & Normalization
5. Technical Schema
6. Backend & DB Sync
7. Performance Budget
8. License Compliance

The audit is intended as a factual pre-flight checklist.
It should expose failures and evidence rather than inventing a subjective overall score.
A design can be visually attractive and still fail technical, responsive, asset, or licensing checks.


# 21. DEMO MODE

1. Competition Brief Ingestion
2. AI Deconstruction
3. Structured Research

7. AI Assistant Multi-Review

Controls include:

The documented auto-play pacing is 3.5 seconds per step.


# 22. JUDGE PRESENTATION
DemoPresentation is intended to hide editor clutter and present the actual product experience.
The presentation can showcase:
- live 3D visual models;
- GIS/telemetry visuals;
- audit scorecards;
- competition workflow progress.

ExplainabilityPanel answers the question "Why This Design?" for:
- theme;
- layout;
- asset;
- GIS map;
- visual hierarchy;
- uncertainty.

Evidence/source labels include:
- SYSTEM HEURISTIC
- GEMINI ANALYSIS
- RESEARCH
- UNCERTAINTY

AITransparencyCard exposes Design, Strategy, and UX assistant status.


# 23. EXPORT AND HANDOFF
CompetitionExportEngine provides:
- self-contained project JSON package export;
- full canvas state;
- metadata;
- version history;
- import validation;
- restore capability;
- formatted Markdown submission report.

The exported project should be sufficient for transferring a competition artifact without manually reconstructing every configuration step.
When moving the repository to another laptop, source code plus workspace artifacts remain the primary portable state.


# PHASE 1–8 — Foundation through competition intelligence
The early phases established the Armory's design/canvas foundation, asset intelligence, visual kits, competition brief analysis, visual strategy, validators, command center, and initial AI assistant abstraction.
Phase 8 specifically introduced Competition Intelligence & AI Assistant Layer.
The Phase 8 pipeline was:
competition prompt -> BriefAnalyzer -> VisualStrategyGenerator -> VisualKitEngine -> AI review board + DesignValidator -> LiveCanvas.
Verification note: Phase 8 reported successful build and scenario verification.

# PHASE 9 — Real Gemini AI Competition Copilot
Phase 9 added GeminiAIProvider, AIChangeValidator, Ask the Armory, provider badges, structured Gemini responses, and automatic MockAI fallback.
The key guarantee became:
AI advises -> Armory validates -> User decides -> PixelComposer renders.
Verification note: Phase 9 reported validator, provider, Ask the Armory, competition check, and asset integrity tests.

# PHASE 10 — Production backend, secure Gemini bridge, research, project/version system
Phase 10 introduced the server backend, MySQL schema, server-side Gemini bridge, research quadrants, project manager, version snapshots, visual diffs, and the eight-dimension audit.
The backend became the persistence and secure AI bridge layer.
Verification note: Phase 10 reported 33/33 tests, lint pass, and production build pass.

# PHASE 11 — End-to-end workflow integration
Phase 11 unified the existing systems under CompetitionWorkflowEngine and connected brief intake, research, strategy, assets, draft generation, live canvas, AI review, guarded mutation, persistence, snapshots, and final audit.
Verification note: Phase 11 reported 37/37 tests plus Phase 10 regression success.

# PHASE 12 — Stress testing and production hardening
Phase 12 added ten canonical competition simulations, stronger AI sanitization, section clamping, strict registry validation, isolated assistant failures, and vendor code splitting.
Verification note: Phase 12 reported 62/62 phase tests and 132/132 cumulative tests.

# PHASE 13 — Deployment, demo, presentation, export
Phase 13 added production environment modes, health/readiness/liveness probes, 12-step demo mode, judge presentation, explainability, AI transparency, and export/import.
Verification note: Phase 13 reported 48/48 phase tests and 180/180 cumulative tests.

# PHASE 14 — Isolated workspace and competition project environment
Phase 14 created WORKSPACE/ as the isolated creative environment inside the repository.
WORKSPACE/COMPETITIONS/ holds competition projects.
WORKSPACE/UI_UX_WORK/ holds ordinary UI/UX work.
WORKSPACE/EXPERIMENTS/ holds technical/layout spikes.
WORKSPACE/RESEARCH/ holds research dossiers.
WORKSPACE/ARCHIVE/ holds preserved past submissions.
Competition templates contain separate ROUND_1 and ROUND_2 trees.
Verification note: Phase 14 reported 62/62 phase tests and 242/242 cumulative tests.

# 24. WORKSPACE PHILOSOPHY
WORKSPACE is intentionally separate from the core Armory code.
It lives inside the repository but is treated as an isolated project area.
The objective is to prevent competition-specific prototypes from changing the platform itself.
The core Armory should remain reusable across competitions.
Each competition gets its own project directory.
Each project has its own metadata and round folders.


# 25. WORKSPACE STRUCTURE
WORKSPACE/
COMPETITIONS/
  _TEMPLATE/
    ROUND_1/
    ROUND_2/
  <competition-project>/
UI_UX_WORK/
  _TEMPLATE/
  <uiux-projects>/
EXPERIMENTS/
RESEARCH/
ARCHIVE/

The actual current directory names should be verified in the repository.
Phase 14 documented this hierarchy and a WorkspaceManager/workspaceTypes layer for structural validation.


# 26. COMPETITION PROJECT METADATA
The documented project.json convention supports:
- competition round;
- project identity;
- versioning from v0.1 through v2.0;
- audit scores/metadata;
- traceability.

The exact current JSON schema should be read from the workspace implementation before writing new metadata.
Do not invent incompatible project.json fields when a current schema exists.


# 27. TWO-ROUND COMPETITION MODEL
The competition has two rounds.
Round 1 is not merely a disposable prototype.
Round 1 should produce a stable, documented baseline.
Once Round 1 is submitted, preserve its final state as immutable evidence.
Round 2 starts from the accepted Round 1 baseline and introduces the new round's requirements and feedback.

Recommended lifecycle:
ROUND 1:
Brief -> Research -> References -> Concept -> UI/UX -> Prototype -> AI Review -> Iteration -> Testing -> Final -> Submission.

ROUND 2:
Round 1 Final Snapshot -> Round 2 Brief/Feedback -> Critique -> New Research -> Redesign -> Advanced Prototype -> AI Review -> Responsive Testing -> Final Audit -> Presentation -> Submission.

The system must preserve:
- what existed at the end of Round 1;
- what changed in Round 2;
- why it changed;
- which requirements caused the change;
- which AI recommendations were accepted or rejected;
- which versions were used for final submission.


# 28. ROUND 1 FREEZE RULE
After Round 1 finalization, create a named immutable snapshot.
Suggested conceptual name:
ROUND_1_FINAL_SUBMISSION_BASELINE.

Do not overwrite it during Round 2.
Any Round 2 change must occur in Round 2 directories/version records.
This protects against accidental loss of the original submission.


# 29. ROUND 2 FEEDBACK RULE
When Round 2 starts, treat the Round 1 final artifact as an input.
Do not automatically assume every Round 1 design decision should remain.
For each major change, record:
- original state;
- problem/feedback;
- proposed change;
- evidence;
- AI input if used;
- human decision;
- resulting version.
This creates a defensible design evolution story for judges.


# 30. HOW TO USE ARMORY FOR A NEW COMPETITION
Step 1: Create a competition directory under WORKSPACE/COMPETITIONS/.
Step 2: Copy the current competition template.
Step 3: Record the competition name and round structure in project.json.
Step 4: Put the raw prompt in ROUND_1/01_BRIEF/.
Step 5: Run BriefAnalyzer/competition workflow.
Step 6: Preserve research outputs.
Step 7: Generate the first visual strategy.
Step 8: Select registered assets.
Step 9: Generate the first draft.
Step 10: Inspect desktop/tablet/mobile.
Step 11: Run AI review.
Step 12: Apply only validated mutations.
Step 13: Snapshot meaningful milestones.
Step 14: Run the eight-dimension audit.
Step 15: Prepare demo/presentation.
Step 16: Export the project and submission report.

# 33. PERFORMANCE HARDENING
Phase 12 introduced production code splitting in vite.config.ts.
Documented vendor chunks included:
- three;
- r3f;
- framer;
- leaflet;
- lucide.

The documented core application bundle reached approximately 73.95 kB gzipped in the Phase 12 report.
The purpose of splitting is to keep heavy 3D/UI/map dependencies out of the core application chunk.
Do not remove manual chunking without measuring the resulting bundle.


# 34. SECURITY MODEL
Security boundaries include:
- server-side secret storage in the later architecture;
- sanitized production errors;
- strict AI mutation validation;
- registry-based asset selection;
- theme/layout whitelisting;
- HTML/script sanitization;
- section count clamping;
- no arbitrary executable code from AI;
- health endpoints without secret leakage;
- production-safe startup diagnostics.

The AI model is an untrusted recommendation source.
The validator is a trusted policy layer.
The renderer should consume validated configuration rather than arbitrary model text.


# 35. HEALTH AND DEPLOYMENT
Phase 13 added:
GET /api/health
GET /api/health/readiness
GET /api/health/liveness

Health response metadata can include:
status;
database;
gemini;
persistence;
version;
uptime;
timestamp.

Readiness indicates whether the service can serve.
Liveness indicates whether the process is alive.
Production errors suppress raw internal stack traces.
Environment modes are development, production, and test.


# 36. AI RESEARCH BRIDGE
The research bridge separates output into four quadrants:
FACT
ANALYSIS
RECOMMENDATION
UNCERTAINTY

FACT should contain grounded statements.
ANALYSIS should explain implications.
RECOMMENDATION should propose concrete configuration or design actions.
UNCERTAINTY should explicitly identify assumptions or unknowns.

Source metadata can include credibility labels such as:
verified
official
inferred

Never collapse uncertainty into fact.
Never present an AI recommendation as an objective requirement unless the competition brief or evidence supports it.


# 37. COMMON FAILURE MODES
Failure mode: inventing a 3D asset ID.
Correct behavior: query assetRegistry and use only registered IDs.

Failure mode: letting Gemini write React code.
Correct behavior: request structured configuration mutation and validate it.

Failure mode: modifying the core Armory for a one-off competition.
Correct behavior: work inside WORKSPACE/COMPETITIONS/<project>.

Failure mode: overwriting Round 1 while preparing Round 2.
Correct behavior: freeze Round 1 and branch into Round 2.

Failure mode: assuming MySQL must always be online.
Correct behavior: preserve and test fallback persistence.

Failure mode: treating Gemini as always available.
Correct behavior: maintain MockAI/local fallback.

Failure mode: trusting an audit score without evidence.
Correct behavior: inspect the underlying criteria.

Failure mode: declaring a prototype complete because the page renders.
Correct behavior: check requirements, responsive behavior, asset integrity, technical schema, backend state, performance, and licensing.

10. Run npm run lint.
11. Run npm run build.
12. Run the latest relevant test suite.
13. Do not start Phase 15 automatically.
14. Do not restructure the repository automatically.
15. Ask for the actual competition brief when beginning a competition prototype.


# 41. FRESH AGENT SYSTEM PROMPT
You are now working inside the existing Pixelcraft Armory repository.
Your first duty is to understand before modifying.
Read PROJECT_CONTEXT_MASTER.md and the phase documentation.
Treat source code as the implementation authority.
Preserve existing architecture.
Use WORKSPACE/ for actual prototypes.
Never place one-off competition code into the core Armory unless explicitly requested.
Never invent asset IDs, theme IDs, layout IDs, or API contracts.
Never allow AI output to execute arbitrary code.
Use AIChangeValidator for AI configuration mutations.
Use CompetitionWorkflowEngine for the end-to-end competition path.
Use apiClient for persistence communication.
Use DemoModeController and CompetitionExportEngine for presentation/handoff.
Maintain Round 1 and Round 2 separation.
Run lint/build/tests after modifications.
Document important changes.
If uncertain, inspect the relevant source file before deciding.

# 44. CHANGE CONTROL RULES
Rule 1: Reuse before replacing.
Rule 2: Extend before duplicating.
Rule 3: Validate before mutating.
Rule 4: Snapshot before risky changes.
Rule 5: Keep competition artifacts outside core source.
Rule 6: Preserve Round 1 before Round 2.
Rule 7: Test shared infrastructure against regressions.
Rule 8: Never hardcode secrets.
Rule 9: Never trust AI-generated identifiers without registry validation.
Rule 10: Never call a design complete without the required audit.

# 47. TROUBLESHOOTING
If the frontend does not build:
- run npm run lint;
- inspect the first TypeScript error;
- inspect imports and aliases;
- avoid fixing unrelated warnings by rewriting large modules.

If the backend does not start:
- inspect environment variables;
- check port configuration;
- check database connectivity;
- verify that fallback persistence is still enabled.

If Gemini is unavailable:
- verify the server-side GEMINI_API_KEY configuration;
- check the health endpoint;
- confirm MockAI/local fallback;
- do not expose the key to the client.

If an AI mutation is rejected:
- inspect the validator error;
- confirm the proposed asset/theme/layout exists in the registry;
- inspect whether the mutation path is whitelisted;
- do not weaken the validator merely to accept hallucinated output.

If a 3D model overflows:
- inspect model fitting/normalization;
- use the existing registered model;
- adjust validated visual size/framing rather than replacing the asset with an unregistered model.

If a competition prototype breaks:
- check the workspace project version;
- restore the last known-good snapshot;
- inspect semantic diff;
- then apply the smallest corrective change.


# 48. SOURCE OF TRUTH HIERARCHY
When information conflicts, use this order:
1. Current source code and current runtime behavior.
2. Current tests.
3. Current phase documentation.
4. Current workspace project metadata.
5. Historical phase reports.
6. This master context document.
7. General model knowledge.

Historical reports describe what was implemented at that time.
They do not override current code.
This master document intentionally records some historical transitions, especially the Phase 9 client-side Gemini key path versus the later Phase 10 server-side secret isolation.


# 49. WHAT IS IMPLEMENTED VS WHAT IS A GOAL
Implemented/documented:
- layered AI provider architecture;
- Gemini provider;
- MockAI fallback;
- AIChangeValidator;
- CompetitionWorkflowEngine;
- backend REST architecture;
- MySQL schema;
- in-memory fallback;
- LocalStorage resilience;
- structured research;
- project/version system;
- semantic version diff;
- eight-dimension audit;
- competition simulation;
- production health probes;
- demo mode;
- explainability;
- export/import;
- workspace isolation;
- two-round workspace templates.

Goals/operational expectations:
- using the system to build a particular future competition prototype;
- adapting the workspace to the actual competition brief;
- adding new competition-specific assets only when legitimately needed;
- any future Phase 15+ capabilities.

Do not claim a future competition-specific feature already exists until it has been implemented and tested.


# 50. FINAL HANDOFF INSTRUCTION
A fresh Antigravity instance should treat this repository as a mature competition prototyping platform.
The correct next action is not to rebuild Pixelcraft Armory.
The correct next action is to understand the existing platform, select/create the appropriate WORKSPACE project, ingest the actual competition brief, and use the existing workflow to build the prototype.
The two-round event lifecycle must remain visible in project structure and version history.
Round 1 should be preserved as the baseline.
Round 2 should be an explicit evolution with its own evidence and final audit.
The Armory remains the reusable tool.
The workspace contains the work produced by the tool.


# 51.GLOSSARY.ARMORY.001
Term: Armory
Definition: The reusable design and competition assembly platform.
Usage rule: inspect the current implementation before relying on undocumented details.
Boundary rule: do not bypass neighboring validation or persistence layers.
Transfer rule: when moving to another laptop, preserve the source tree and workspace data.
